title: The Cappadocians
hook: Basil and the two Gregorys gave the words for three persons in one being

segments.voice: Yesterday, On the Incarnation: Athanasius and the portrait redrawn on the same wood. Your line was a king in the city. Which street did you walk with that picture? Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

Ask the money-changer for change, and he lectures you about the Begotten and the Unbegotten. Ask the baker the price of bread, and he tells you the Father is greater and the Son is less. Ask whether the bath is ready, and the attendant informs you that the Son was made from nothing. That's Gregory of Nyssa, in a sermon, complaining about a great city where everyone seemed to have an opinion about God. The arguments over the Trinity weren't happening only in libraries. They were happening at the market. Today, the people who sharpened the church's words: the Cappadocians.

Cappadocia is a region in what is now central Turkey. From there came Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus. Gregory of Nyssa also wrote about their sister Macrina as a teacher in her own right. The question they faced was old. Jesus sends his disciples out baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." One name, three named. And Paul's blessing names all three together. So is God one or three? The Cappadocians answered with two Greek words, and gave each a separate job. Ousia, being: what God is. There is one. Hypostasis, person: who God is. There are three, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. One being, three persons. Not three gods working as a team. Not one God wearing three masks. They offered comparisons, like three people sharing one human nature, and then warned that every comparison falls short, because God is not one more thing in the world. Gregory of Nazianzus put the experience of it this way, in paraphrase: no sooner do I think of the One than I'm lit up by the Three; no sooner do I tell the Three apart than I'm carried back to the One. Their words helped shape how the Nicene Creed came to be understood. For them, the Trinity was not a puzzle to solve. It was a mystery to stand inside.
screen: `LIT BY THE THREE, BACK TO THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one God in three persons. Settle, and breathe. Christians have an old blessing from Paul that names all three: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." If you pray, you can say it slowly, letting each name land. Grace. Love. Communion. If you don't pray, just listen to the shape of it: three names, one blessing, given to everyone at once. Breathe between the phrases, and notice how they belong together. The bell holds the time.
The Cappadocians. Basil and the two Gregorys, who helped give the church its words for the Trinity: one being, three persons.

Your line: three and one. Today, notice one thing that's both one and more than one, a family, a team, a chord, and remember the Cappadocians said every comparison falls short. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Churches confess one God in three persons in the Nicene Creed, baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and close prayers and blessings by naming all three; Orthodox and Catholic churches honor Basil and the two Gregorys as saints and teachers.

fork.setup: someone at the market asks you: is God one, or three? what do you answer?
options: one. the three are just masks.
fork.reveal: the Cappadocians helped give the church those words: one ousia, being, and three hypostases, persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

original.note: Greek: being, what God is. the Cappadocians spoke of one ousia in three hypostases, persons.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Trinity means three gods, or one God wearing three masks.
what it means: one God, one being, in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God.
what a scholar hears: ousia and hypostasis, two Greek words the Cappadocians gave separate jobs: one for what God is, one for who.

notes: Hook paraphrases Gregory of Nyssa's well-known complaint about money-changers, bakers and bath attendants debating Begotten/Unbegotten (On the Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit); confirm source and that it was about Constantinople (script says only 'a great city').

Ousia/hypostasis distinction attributed to the Cappadocians; the analogy of three people sharing one human nature appears in Basil's letters (Letter 38 is sometimes attributed to Gregory of Nyssa). Confirm.
Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 40.41 ('No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the splendour of the Three...') paraphrased; confirm.
Macrina 'as a teacher in her own right' rests on Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina and On the Soul and the Resurrection, where she is called 'the teacher'; confirm.
'Their words fed the Nicene Creed that churches still say' refers to the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (Council of Constantinople); no date given. Confirm phrasing.
howItsDone softened from 'many prayers' to 'prayers and blessings'.

Editor pass: Cappadocia located 'in what is now central Turkey' (not 'in the hills'); 'the Nicene Creed that churches still say' (sweeping claim) became 'helped shape how the Nicene Creed came to be understood'; tense fixed in the closing line.

Audit pass: "gave the church its words" (overstated: ousia and hypostasis had earlier users, Athanasius among them) softened to "sharpened" / "helped give" in hook, word and fork. howItsDone named only Orthodox churches as honoring the three; Catholics honor them as saints too (Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus as Doctors of the Church), so both are named.
